content.title: About
content.content: Tamale, no meat is a traditional Mexican dish made from corn masa dough and a filling of vegetables, beans, cheese and spices, wrapped in corn husks (or banana leaves) and steamed until cooked. It has a gentle corn aroma, a slightly sweet base flavor and a rich, savory spice profile.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tamales are among the oldest dishes in the Americas, prepared by the Maya and Aztec civilizations.
They are traditionally served at celebrations and holidays, especially Day of the Dead and Christmas.
Corn husks used for wrapping impart a distinctive aroma and keep the tamale shape during steaming.
There are countless regional variations, from sweet fruit‑filled to spicy chili‑and‑cheese versions.
The vegetarian, meat‑free version has gained popularity in recent decades with the rise of plant‑based diets.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Corn masa provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Tamales deliver slowly digestible carbohydrates that help maintain steady energy levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain thiamine, niacin and folate, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Plant protein
items.content: Beans and cheese in the filling supply a complete set of essential amino acids for vegetarians.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Corn and vegetables contain carotenoids and vitamin C, which help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Fillings seasoned with soy sauce or salty cheeses can be high in salt.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Tamales are moderately calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: If not cooled promptly, steamed tamales can spoil quickly; they should be refrigerated within two hours of cooking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tamales are typically served hot, unwrapped from the corn husk. Eat them as a main dish or with salsa, guacamole, or sour cream. For a fresh touch, add chopped cilantro, lime juice, and sliced avocado.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked tamales in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a freezer‑safe bag; reheat by steaming for 10‑15 minutes or microwaving with a splash of water.
